o: We choose a set of nodes to invert; inverting a node negates every value in its subtree, and any two inverted nodes must be at graph distance >= k. We want the maximum resulting total sum. Key observations: a node's final sign is (-1)^(number of inverted strict ancestors), and whether we may invert a node depends only on the distance to the nearest inverted strict ancestor. So a rooted DFS state needs just two pieces of information flowing from ancestors: that nearest-inverted-ancestor distance (capped at k, since anything >= k behaves identically) and the parity of inverted ancestors. Example 4 shows why the cap matters: with k = 3 we cannot invert both leaves (distance 2), so inverting the root is optimal.
k: A node's sign depends only on the parity of inverted ancestors; its eligibility to be inverted depends only on the distance to the nearest inverted ancestor, capped at k.
Distances >= k are equivalent, so the distance dimension has only k+1 values, giving O(n*k) states.
When we invert node u, all children start with distance 1 and flipped parity; otherwise children inherit distance min(d+1, k) and unchanged parity.

a.n: Approach 1: Tree DP over (node, capped distance, parity)
a.i: Define dp[u][d][p] = maximum sum achievable in the subtree of u, given that the nearest inverted strict ancestor is at distance d (capped at k, d = k means none nearby enough to matter) and p is the parity of inverted ancestors. At u we either skip (children get d' = min(d+1, k), same p) or invert u — allowed only if d >= k — giving u a negated value and children d' = 1, p' = p XOR 1. Processing nodes in reverse BFS order evaluates this bottom-up without recursion-depth issues.
s: Build adjacency, compute a BFS order and parent array from the root.
Initialize dp[u][d][p] for leaves: max(nums[u] * sign(p), and if d >= k, -nums[u] * sign(p)).
Process nodes in reverse BFS order: for each state, skip-option sums children's dp[c][min(d+1,k)][p]; invert-option (if d >= k) negates nums[u] and sums children's dp[c][1][p^1]; take the max.
Return dp[0][k][0] (root has no inverted ancestors).
a.t: O(n * k) — each of the n nodes evaluates 2(k+1) states, each scanning its children a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n * k) for the DP table plus O(n) for the BFS order and parents.

w: This DP formulation is essentially the unique efficient approach, so spend interview time justifying the state: why capping distance at k is safe (a candidate inverted ancestor farther than k imposes no additional restriction) and why parity fully determines signs. Implement iteratively (reverse BFS order) rather than recursively — a path-shaped tree with n = 5*10^4 will blow the default stack in several languages. Edge cases: k = 1 (every pair of distinct nodes is far enough, so greedily negate every negative-value leaf-heavy structure is NOT valid reasoning — trust the DP), negative nums values, and the root itself being invertible. A common follow-up asks to output which nodes to invert; store argmax choices during the DP.
